notes.meaning: In the early generations after the flood, all people on earth spoke the exact same language and used the same words. Because everyone understood one another, they could easily communicate and work together on common projects.

As the human family moved across the region, they came to a wide, fertile plain in southern Mesopotamia called Shinar. Instead of spreading out to fill the earth as God had instructed Noah's family, they chose to settle together in one place.

The people agreed together to mold clay bricks and bake them thoroughly in fire to make them strong. The plain lacked stone and mortar, so they used these kiln-fired bricks and joined them with sticky tar, also known as bitumen.

The people set out to build a great city and a towering structure reaching toward the sky to win lasting fame for themselves. They hoped this massive project would keep them united and secure, directly defying God's plan for them to spread across the earth.

differ.view: The project was an act of total human rebellion where men sought earthly glory rather than depending on God's grace.
The tower was designed as an idolatrous temple to heavenly bodies, marking an organized religious revolt against the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The text serves as a critique of ancient Mesopotamian building traditions, where building one massive city violated the mandate to populate the wider world.

notes.meaning: The Lord came down to look over the city and the tower that the people were constructing. The Bible describes God this way in human terms to show that even humanity's grandest achievements look small from heaven.

The Lord observed that the people shared one language and a single purpose, which meant their rebellious plans would quickly go unchecked. If their sinful ambitions were left without limits, evil would spread rapidly.

God decided to confuse their speech so that they could no longer understand what each other was saying. When God says 'let Us,' Christian teachers have traditionally seen a glimpse of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—counseling together.

Because the builders could not communicate, they abandoned their work on the city. The Lord scattered them across the surface of the earth, fulfilling His original purpose for humanity through this act of judgment.

differ.view: The scattering of languages judged human pride while also dividing nations so their competing ambitions would restrain global evil.

notes.meaning: The city was called Babel because the Lord confused the languages of the people there and scattered them around the globe. The name sounds like the Hebrew word for confusion, turning man's boastful project into a lasting sign of human weakness.

Shem became the father of Arphaxad two years after the flood when he was one hundred years old, and he lived another five hundred years raising other children. This genealogy traces the godly line from Noah down toward the family of Abraham.
Arphaxad was thirty-five years old when Shelah was born, and he lived four hundred and three more years. The family records show that human lifespans were gradually growing shorter after the flood.

Shelah was thirty years old when his son Eber was born, and he lived another four hundred and three years with more sons and daughters. Through Eber, this chosen family continued down through history.

Eber was thirty-four years old when he became the father of Peleg, living four hundred and thirty years after that. Peleg's name means division, pointing to the period when mankind was divided and scattered across the earth.
Peleg lived thirty years before his son Reu was born, and he lived two hundred and nine years after that. Lifespans dropped even more sharply during these generations.
Reu lived thirty-two years before fathering Serug, and he lived another two hundred and seven years. The record steadily moves through the centuries toward God's covenant with Abraham.
Serug was thirty years old when his son Nahor was born, and he lived another two hundred years with other sons and daughters. Serug was the great-grandfather of Abram.
Nahor lived twenty-nine years before fathering Terah, and he lived another one hundred and nineteen years. By this time, patriarchs were living shorter lives, under one hundred and fifty years.
Terah lived seventy years before fathering Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Abram is named first because of his importance in God's promises, even though he was not necessarily the firstborn son.

This passage introduces the family line of Terah, who was the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran, and records that Haran was the father of Lot. These family members play important roles in the stories that follow.
Haran died while his father Terah was still alive, in their home city of Ur of the Chaldeans. Ur was a large city in southern Mesopotamia where the surrounding culture worshiped idols and false gods.

Abram married Sarai, and his brother Nahor married his niece Milcah, who was the daughter of their late brother Haran. Marrying within the extended family was common at that time and kept their households closely knit.
Sarai was unable to have children. This detail highlights human helplessness, setting up the miraculous way God would later fulfill His promise to give Abram descendants.

Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot, and Abram's wife Sarai, and set out from Ur of the Chaldeans toward the land of Canaan. Instead of going all the way, they stopped in the northern commercial city of Haran and made their home there.

differ.view: Stopping in Haran represented incomplete obedience, showing that Abram delayed full compliance with God's call until his father died.

notes.meaning: Terah lived two hundred and five years and died while still in Haran. His death brought an end to the family's delay, preparing the way for Abram to obey God's call and continue his journey into Canaan.
